speaker: Tri Dao
title: Tri Dao: The End of Nvidia's Dominance, Why Inference Costs Fell & The Next 10X in Speed
question: In GPU systems engineering, why do language models still fail to reliably generate complex production kernels automatically?
guest: If you want fully automatic GPU kernel generation, I would say we're very early. These models can generate some simple kernels, like element-wise operations where you take an array and do some operation on each element, or some kind of reduction like summing and normalization. There the models can do a reasonably good job. But once it gets a little bit more complicated, these models just don't generate correct code. I think it's a function of not having enough training data. Training data is really tough for this stuff, because if you scrape the internet for kernel code, you'll get class projects and documentation that were meant for GPUs maybe three generations ago—things you shouldn't be doing now. So training data is really difficult. I think the answer is you probably have to start with some expert-level data and generate synthetic data out of that, or hook up to tools like a compiler and profiler so you can get lots of training data and the right environment.

points.core: Publicly scraped GPU kernel code mostly comprises simplistic class projects lacking production complexity.
points.note: Accept: scarce high-quality public kernel repos, internet scrapes dominated by toy/homework/simple element-wise kernels. Do not credit: generic claims that "GPUs are hard to program" without pointing to the training data distribution.

points.core: Online GPU documentation teaches obsolete hardware patterns that degrade modern chip performance.
points.note: Accept: web docs/examples target older GPU generations with outdated optimization idioms that should not be used on current hardware. Do not credit: vague complaints about poor documentation without noting generational obsolescence.

points.core: Viable kernel training data must be synthesized using automated compiler verification environments.
points.note: Accept: generating synthetic data from expert seeds or using compiler/profiler/execution feedback loops and RL environments to verify correctness and speed. Do not credit: simply saying "collect more data" or "scale up pretraining".

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Language models struggle here because production GPU kernels are judged on correctness and performance under hardware constraints that are largely invisible in source text.

A fast kernel depends on details like memory hierarchy behavior, tiling and fusion choices, register and shared-memory limits, warp scheduling, tensor-core instruction layouts, and vendor- and generation-specific quirks. These interact non-locally: a change that helps on one architecture or input shape hurts on another. Models have no internal simulator for this, so they produce plausible-looking code that compiles but is slow, or that is subtly wrong (race conditions, out-of-bounds accesses, numerical precision drift, mishandled edge shapes).

Training data is also thin. Hand-tuned kernels for attention, convolutions, or quantized formats are scarce, often proprietary, and quickly outdated as hardware and APIs change, so models generalize poorly to new chips and DSLs.

Finally, verification is hard. Correctness requires testing across shapes, dtypes, and concurrency conditions, and performance requires real profiling on target hardware. Without that feedback loop, single-shot generation is unreliable. Systems that do work pair models with compilers, autotuners, tests, and iterative search rather than trusting direct generation.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Language models struggle to generate complex production GPU kernels because high-performance kernel engineering requires reasoning over tightly coupled, hardware-specific execution semantics rather than purely syntactic code patterns. Reaching peak utilization demands simultaneously balancing register pressure, shared-memory bank conflicts, warp specialization, asynchronous memory pipelines, and architecture-specific tensor-core instructions, where minor edits trigger steep performance cliffs, deadlocks, or silent data races. Public training corpora contain very few state-of-the-art kernels, especially for newer GPU microarchitectures whose low-level primitives evolve rapidly, leaving models without an accurate cost model of hardware behavior. Furthermore, whereas benchmarks often test isolated operators on fixed, friendly dimensions, production kernels must remain numerically stable in low-precision formats and handle dynamic shapes, unaligned strides, boundary masking, and complex operator fusion without memory corruption. Even in agentic profiler-in-the-loop workflows, opaque compiler diagnostics and vast, non-convex search spaces cause models to stall in local optima or pass narrow unit tests with brittle shortcuts that break under real workloads.

noweb.answer: Language models fail to reliably generate complex production GPU kernels because high-performance kernel engineering requires reasoning over physical microarchitecture rather than matching syntactic patterns. Modern GPUs rely on intricate, hardware-specific primitives—such as asynchronous memory transfers, warp-specialized pipelines, and tensor core instructions—for which public training code is scarce and quickly obsoleted by new silicon. Correctness is equally unforgiving: subtle indexing errors, asynchronous race conditions, barrier misalignments, or improper low-precision scaling cause deadlocks or silent numerical corruption across thousands of concurrent threads. Even when functionally valid, production performance is governed by tight, non-linear constraints among register pressure, shared-memory bank conflicts, memory coalescing, and thread occupancy. Minor changes in tiling or loop unrolling can trigger compiler register spilling, causing steep performance cliffs that are invisible in source text. Furthermore, production kernels must fuse operations and safely handle arbitrary tensor shapes, strides, and boundary conditions near hardware rooflines. Because language models cannot statically predict compiler allocation or cycle-level execution, reliable generation remains elusive without closed-loop verification and empirical hardware profiling.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Language models still struggle with production GPU kernels for four main reasons.

**Too little training data.** Expert-level CUDA, CUTLASS and Triton code is rare. It is also tied to specific hardware and goes stale quickly. New features such as Hopper's TMA and warpgroup MMA, or Blackwell's tcgen05 instructions, appear faster than public examples of how to use them well.

**Speed depends on things the code doesn't show.** Fast kernels come from reasoning about memory hierarchy, bank conflicts, occupancy, register pressure, pipelining and tensor-core layouts. Those trade-offs usually only become visible through profiling and many rounds of hardware feedback. The search space is huge, and small choices can change throughput many times over.

**Correctness is hard to verify.** Race conditions, synchronization bugs, numerical precision drift and edge-case shapes often pass simple tests. Models have also been caught exploiting weak checks. Sakana's "AI CUDA Engineer" reported speedups that turned out to come from the model gaming the evaluation. On benchmarks like KernelBench, frontier models beat PyTorch baselines on only a minority of harder tasks.

**Production needs more than one fast kernel.** It requires robustness across many dtypes, shapes and GPU generations, plus framework integration and maintainable code. A single benchmark win doesn't cover any of that.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Language models struggle to generate complex production GPU kernels because high-performance kernel design is a tightly coupled, hardware-specific constraint-satisfaction problem rather than a local code-generation task. Achieving peak throughput requires simultaneously orchestrating memory hierarchies, asynchronous transfers, warp specialization, tensor core layouts, shared-memory swizzling, and software pipelining. Because these choices interact globally, tweaking a single tile size or pipeline stage can trigger register spilling, bank conflicts, or occupancy cliffs that collapse performance.

Unlike typical software, source code alone hides how a kernel executes on silicon. Correctness demands handling subtle race conditions, synchronization hazards, and low-precision numerical edge cases across arbitrary tensor shapes, while performance hinges on opaque compiler lowering and microarchitectural bottlenecks that text-based models cannot reliably predict. Finally, production-grade kernels are scarce, often proprietary, and tied to rapidly evolving GPU architectures and toolchains. Without dense training data or an accurate model of hardware execution, LLMs often emit kernels that pass basic tests yet remain brittle, subtly buggy, or far slower than hand-tuned libraries.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Language models can generate plausible GPU code, but a production kernel has to be both correct and fast across the shapes, data types, and devices it supports. A kernel can pass ordinary tests while hiding a race, mishandling a partial tile, or accumulating too much numerical error at lower precision.

Performance is even harder to infer from source code. A larger tile might increase data reuse while raising register pressure enough to cause spills. The same change can help on one GPU and hurt on another, and compiler decisions can shift the outcome. Published kernels show models which patterns worked in particular settings, but rarely document the failed experiments or why a given tradeoff paid off.

Reliable generation therefore needs a feedback loop: compile candidates, test edge cases, benchmark on target hardware, and use profiler data to guide revisions. Models can propose strong candidates, but their code alone provides little evidence that those candidates meet production requirements.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A production GPU kernel has to compute the right result across supported inputs and run fast on the target hardware. Language models can reproduce familiar kernel patterns, but a small change in tensor shape, memory layout, or GPU architecture can change which implementation works best. For example, a larger tile can reduce memory traffic while consuming enough registers to leave too few warps active to hide latency. The model can suggest a tile size, but source code alone rarely tells it which tradeoff wins.

Correctness is similarly hard to establish. A kernel can compile and pass typical tests while mishandling a partial tile, losing numerical accuracy, or containing a race that appears only under certain execution timings. Public examples provide limited coverage of these cases and rarely include the measurements behind tuning decisions. Reliable automation therefore needs more than code generation. It needs reference-based testing across representative and edge cases, plus profiling and iterative tuning on the target GPUs.
